problem: 'A good SLA is measurable by both sides' is ambiguous; it can be read as 'both sides can measure something different' rather than both parties measuring the same metric the same way.
fix: A good SLA can be measured the same way by both parties: same metric, same window, same data source.

problem: The SLA is described only as what the provider promises. Standard SLAs also set duties on the customer (paying on time, not misusing the service, reporting incidents) and that gap can mislead a student who thinks an SLA is one-sided.
fix: Add: the SLA also lists what the customer must do, such as paying on time and reporting faults through the agreed channel.

problem: The nines list stops at 99.9%, but the chapter uses 99.95% everywhere (SLO and worked example) without ever saying it is 'three and a half nines'.
fix: Add: 99.95% is three and a half nines, with allowed unavailability 0.0005.

problem: 'An SLO must be stricter than the SLA' is stated as an absolute law. It is the usual discipline when a customer-facing SLA exists, but internal services often have an SLO and no SLA, and some contracts set the two equal.
fix: 'When there is both, the SLO should normally be stricter than the SLA. If it is looser, the error budget is larger than the contract allows and gives no warning before credits are due.'

problem: The example says flatly that no credits are due. Section 3 correctly says credits depend on the contract terms and on the customer filing a claim in time, so the example should state the assumption it is making.
fix: 'No credits are due, assuming the usual terms: credits follow only an SLA breach, and the customer files the claim inside the stated period.'
